sources.title: How To Quickly Improve Your Backhand Consistency (Pro Tennis Technique)
7 Steps to a Fluid Two-Handed Backhand
How To Hit A Tennis Backhand With Venus Williams
The one-handed backhand: Tennis Masterclass, Episode 5
How To Hit A Tennis Backhand: Simple Tips For a Perfect Backhand

good_form: On the takeback, use a loop or C shape: racket head starts above the hands, hands stay between shoulder and hip.
Let the racket head drop below the hand and below the incoming ball, ideally with the racket face pointing slightly down.
From the drop, pull up and forward to a contact point in front of you (two-handers are a bit less far out than one-handers).
At contact the racket face should be neutral or very slightly closed, giving topspin, net clearance and depth.
On returns, a compact takeback with a block and little or no follow-through is fine because there's no time.
On the forward swing, the non-dominant (left, for righties) arm should be more active and dictate the extension.
Wait to bend the elbows until the left arm is fairly straight, without hyperextending it, so the arm extends long before coming over.
Finish high over the dominant shoulder, with the elbow pointing forward toward the opponent and the butt cap pointing there too.
Use a low base and load the back leg, with a long stride.
Push into the ground and let the energy flow up through the body and forward to get pop on the ball.
Engage the whole body from the ground up, including the left side.

faults.name: Straight down-and-back takeback
faults.looks_like: Taking the racket just down and back, then up to high over the right shoulder, with no loop.
faults.why_it_matters: It's a missed chance for more rhythm, power and control; a loop gives a smoother, rounder motion and more control.
causes: Down and back is easier for newer players
fixes: Use a loop or C shape: racket head above hands, then drop below the hand and ball, then pull up and forward.
Do the drill shown with Carlos Alcaraz to feel what the racket head does in a loop.
Keep the compact down-and-back/block only for returns when time is short.
outcome_effects: Less rhythm, power and control than with a loop

faults.name: Not extending long enough / pulling across the body
faults.looks_like: Pulling the racket across the body on the forward swing and finishing across the hips instead of high.
faults.why_it_matters: It deprives the player of control and power.
causes: Non-dominant arm not active on the forward swing
Bending the elbows too early before the left arm is straightened
fixes: Make the off arm dictate the extension on the forward swing.
Don't start bending the elbows until the left arm is fairly straight, without hyperextending.
Finish high over the right shoulder, with elbow and butt cap pointing toward the opponent.

faults.name: Hitting harder with just the arms
faults.looks_like: Trying to hit a harder ball because there are two hands on the racket, and swinging with the arms only.
faults.why_it_matters: Arm-only hitting tires you over a match and feels jerky, not round, with less ball control.
causes: Believing that two hands on the racket means you should hit a harder ball
fixes: Work on a low base and loading the back leg with a long stride.
Push into the ground and let the energy flow up through the body.
Do the drill with a pull rope fixed slightly below hip height on a fence, engaging the whole body including the left side.

good_form: Keep the non-dominant (left) elbow away from the body, with visible space between elbow and hip/abdomen, as the racket goes back.
Treat the two-handed backhand like a lefty forehand and use the same elbow-to-abdomen spacing rule as on a forehand.
Create the elbow space early, then let the racket drop, find room and swing out to contact.
The space can be created either by pulling the arm back low to high or by taking the racket tip up as on a forehand; either way the elbow needs room from the hip.

faults.name: Non-dominant elbow stuck on the hip
faults.looks_like: During the racket takeback the left elbow sits against the hip or body, with no visible gap between elbow and shirt/torso.
faults.why_it_matters: Space is so limited that even a great follow-through cannot rescue the shot, making an effective two-hander very hard.
causes: Focusing only on leading with the left hand, swinging out to contact, the big finish and the right elbow, while neglecting the left elbow
fixes: On takeback, move the elbow away from the body, as on a forehand
Keep the same elbow-to-abdomen gap as on a forehand
Create the space early, then drop the racket and swing out to contact
outcome_effects: Small, cramped follow-through across the chest

good_form: Take the racket back low rather than high, dropping the elbow toward the rib cage so the racket drops toward the body.
Think of dipping the racket head (head guard) into a pool on the pullback.
Keep the hands relaxed so the swing can flow through to a full follow-through.
Treat the two-handed backhand as a one-handed forehand with the non-dominant (top) hand, with the bottom hand there only for stability.
The top hand (left hand for a righty) should do all the swinging.
The bottom hand should touch the racket just lightly, enough to stop it feeling wobbly at contact.

faults.name: Starting the backswing too high
faults.looks_like: Racket pulled back too high, with the top arm flaring out like a chicken wing.
faults.why_it_matters: It makes you slap at the ball and often hit down on it, so you miss more balls in the net than you should.
causes: Top arm flaring out like a chicken wing, which encourages the high pullback
fixes: Drop the elbow down toward the rib cage so the racket drops toward the body.
Relax the elbow.
Pull the racket back as if dipping it in a pool.

faults.name: Gripping the racket too tight
faults.looks_like: Hands tight on the racket (a death grip), and the swing stops short.
faults.why_it_matters: A tight grip stops a fluid follow-through, which limits racket head speed, spin and power.
causes: Tight hands that don't let the racket swing through
fixes: Relax your hands on the racket.

faults.name: Swinging with the bottom hand
faults.looks_like: On the two-handed backhand, the bottom hand (right hand for a righty) drives the swing and pulls across the body instead of the top hand doing the swinging. The speaker says this is less obvious on camera.
faults.why_it_matters: It makes you pull across the ball and costs you depth.
causes: The bottom hand doing the swinging instead of just stabilizing
fixes: Let the top (non-dominant) hand do all the swinging.
Hold the racket very lightly with the bottom hand, only enough for stability.
Think of the shot as a one-handed forehand with the non-dominant hand.

good_form: Ideal double-handed grip: left hand on bevel 7 and right hand on bevel 2, as Djokovic uses.
Grip means the area from the knuckle through to the palm sits against the bevel, on both hands.
With the left hand on bevel 7 it is strong, does most of the work and lets you swing through the ball.
With both grips right, contact point, arms and hands feel comfortable, and it is easier to hit down the line and crosscourt.
Imagine hitting the ball with your left palm, so the racket becomes one with the palm and the palm goes to the target.
Left hand contacts the ball, then goes through and over; the wrist does not break early, and you release at the end.
Step forward into the ball by going out and then in, getting behind the ball; a closed stance is fine if you step forward.

faults.name: Left hand too far over (bevel 4)
faults.looks_like: Left hand sits on bevel 4, almost like a western left-handed forehand, and the player pulls the racket across.
faults.why_it_matters: The left wrist is weak, so there is no power or swing.
causes: Left-hand grip rotated to bevel 4 instead of 7
Feeling no power behind the ball
fixes: Move the left hand back to bevel 7 with palm behind and knuckle-to-palm on the bevel
Let the left hand do most of the work and swing through
outcome_effects: No swing; player ends up pulling the racket

faults.name: Right hand slipped to bevel 3
faults.looks_like: Right wrist is too loose and players scoop the ball with their wrists, pulling the racket across to compensate.
faults.why_it_matters: The speaker calls scooping very dangerous and uncomfortable, and the shot is not comfortable to brush the ball with.
causes: Right-hand grip on bevel 3 instead of bevel 2
fixes: Return the right hand to bevel 2 so everything molds together
outcome_effects: You might get lucky but it is inconsistent

faults.name: Wristy hitting, breaking the wrist early
faults.looks_like: Player goes wristy and breaks the wrist too soon instead of guiding through with the left palm.
faults.why_it_matters: The left arm can't guide the ball and anything can happen.
causes: Not thinking of the left palm going to the target
Blends with grip problems
fixes: Imagine hitting with the left palm toward the target
Contact, go through and over, then release at the end
Keep the wrist from breaking, as Djokovic does
outcome_effects: Left arm cannot guide the ball

faults.name: Stepping across and getting stuck
faults.looks_like: Player steps across the body and is jammed, unable to swing.
faults.why_it_matters: You cannot reach your full potential on the double-handed backhand if stuck, because you can't swing.
causes: Stepping across instead of getting behind the ball
fixes: Step out and then in, forward to the ball
Get behind the ball

good_form: Stay relaxed in the grip during the turn so the racket can get underneath the ball.
Get under the ball with the butt cap pointing forward when ready to swing, for a crisp fast backhand.
Follow through fully, up and across, with the butt cap pointing forward again at the end.
Use a Continental or Eastern grip on the bottom hand and an Eastern grip on the top hand.
Start with the arms out and good spacing from the body while waiting for the ball.
Split step as the ball is struck, then rotate the upper body while keeping the spacing.
Hit from out in front with the arms extended, not from tucked in close to the body.
Practice by taking the bottom hand off and hitting a left-handed forehand with the top hand, then add the bottom hand back.

faults.name: Squeezing the racket too tight in the turn
faults.looks_like: Gripping the racket very tightly during the turn phase so the racket stays high and can't drop down under the ball; the backhand becomes a pushing motion.
faults.why_it_matters: Without getting under the ball you can't produce a crisp, fast backhand.
causes: Squeezing the racket too tight during the turn
fixes: Relax the grip in the turn so the racket can get under the ball
Get the butt cap pointing forward when ready to go
outcome_effects: Racket can't get underneath the ball

faults.name: Not following through enough
faults.looks_like: After contact the elbow tucks into the body and the racket stops instead of going all the way up; the player believes they have followed through.
faults.why_it_matters: A full follow-through is very important when going through the ball.
causes: Elbow tucked into the body after contact
fixes: Drop the racket head, go through the ball and continue all the way up
Finish with the butt cap pointing forward
Imagine a volleyball under the armpit

faults.name: Wrong grip (death grip)
faults.looks_like: Holding the racket with a grip, especially on the bottom hand, that blocks the player on the backhand side.
faults.why_it_matters: The grip blocks you and prevents getting under the ball or maneuvering it.
causes: Bottom hand is not in Continental or Eastern
Top hand not in Eastern
fixes: Bottom hand Continental or Eastern, top hand Eastern
For beginners, put the racket under the armpit and take it out like a sword to find a grip between Eastern and Continental
outcome_effects: Can't maneuver the ball at contact

faults.name: Elbows tucked in from the start
faults.looks_like: Waiting for the ball with both elbows tucked in, then turning and hitting with the elbows still tucked in close to the body.
faults.why_it_matters: With tucked elbows you can't have a good take-back or a follow-through.
causes: Waiting for the ball with the arms tucked in at the beginning
fixes: Start with the arms out and good spacing
Split step, then rotate the upper body while keeping the spacing
Hit from out away from the body
Practice one-handed left-handed forehand swings with the top hand

good_form: One-handed backhand uses an Eastern or Continental grip.
Two-handed backhand: dominant hand Eastern or semi-western, non-dominant hand Continental.
Start turning the shoulders the instant the ball leaves the opponent's strings, not when it crosses the net or bounces.
One-handed backhand needs more than 22 cm of shoulder turn; two-handed more than 18 cm.
Turn the hips less than the shoulders, so the gap stores elastic energy in the trunk like a pulled bowstring.
Turn until the front shoulder touches the chin.
Mirror drill: turn fully while keeping your eyes locked on your own eyes in the mirror, so the head stays still.
Hit the ball at waist height, slightly in front of the body, with weight moving forward.
Two-handed contact is about 15 in in front of the front foot; one-handed about 2 ft.
Hit higher over the net than you think; Federer averages about 5 in of clearance and Nadal about 7.5 in. This gives more margin, more spin and deeper shots.
If the ball comes at your body, use the step back drill: jump backward and sideways to make space.
Don't hit with the elbows tucked in.
Follow through fully, finishing naturally over the opposite shoulder.
Finish with the racket tip pointing at the sky.

faults.name: Late preparation
faults.looks_like: Shoulders start turning after the ball has crossed the net or bounced, not as it leaves the opponent's racket.
faults.why_it_matters: Late preparation forces a rushed swing, and a rushed swing loses the point.
causes: Waiting to turn until the ball crosses the net or bounces
fixes: Start turning the shoulders the instant the ball leaves the opponent's strings

faults.name: Hips and shoulders turning as one block
faults.looks_like: The hips and shoulders rotate together with no gap between them, so the player swings with the arm.
faults.why_it_matters: With no hip-shoulder gap, no elastic energy is stored in the trunk. Arm swinging loses to body swinging.
causes: Turning the hips as much as the shoulders
fixes: Turn the hips less than the shoulders to build the gap, like pulling back a bowstring

faults.name: Insufficient shoulder turn
faults.looks_like: The front shoulder does not touch the chin at the end of the turn.
faults.why_it_matters: Without enough turn you can't generate real power.
fixes: Turn until the front shoulder touches the chin
Do the mirror drill, turning fully with your eyes fixed on your own eyes to keep the head still

faults.name: Elbows tucked in
faults.looks_like: The ball is hit with the elbows tucked in close to the body, often when the ball is right at you.
faults.why_it_matters: The speaker says never to hit the ball this way.
causes: Ball coming right at the body with no space
fixes: Do the step back drill: jump backward and sideways to create space

faults.name: Stopping the swing at contact
faults.looks_like: The swing is checked or stopped as soon as the ball leaves the strings, like a golfer stopping at impact.
faults.why_it_matters: The follow-through is where spin is applied, direction is locked in and power is finished.
causes: Stopping the swing when the ball leaves the strings
fixes: Let the racket finish naturally over the opposite shoulder
Finish with the racket tip pointing at the sky
outcome_effects: Loss of spin, direction and power

faults.name: Not lifting enough
faults.looks_like: The racket tip points at the net at the end of the swing instead of at the sky.
faults.why_it_matters: It shows the swing did not lift enough.
causes: Not lifting enough through the swing
fixes: End the swing with the racket tip pointing straight at the sky
outcome_effects: Less net clearance, spin and depth

good_form: Get low with bent legs, like a sumo stance, for a stable base that lets you use body weight and rotate the hips.
Come to the ball with weight evenly spread over both legs, then transfer onto the front foot during the shot.
Think of a U shape: go down, move forward through the bottom of the U, then rise up through the ball.
Start low with the front heel down rather than on the toe, then extend upward and through.
Bend the back leg to get lower; this frees the hip so the front hip and knee can move forward and you can rise onto the back toe.
Let body weight transfer lengthen the contact point; extend and hold the ball on the strings for longer.
Let body weight and the long contact generate power, not the arm, which leaves the hand and wrist free to create topspin.
Let the ball come to you; stay calm and don't rush forward or reach for it.
Swing the non-hitting arm back as the racket arm goes forward, with the elbow almost touching behind you and a stretch in the chest, and hold the finish.
The back arm stops over-rotation across the body and gives a linear, balanced swing.
For balls further away, turn then side-step or crossover step, so you reach the ball with your legs and are still low and upright-free when hitting.
Drag the back toe if needed to stay balanced after the transfer.
The racket finishes high, with spin coming from the racket head moving around the hand, not from lifting the arm.
On wide balls, rotate out through the legs while the left arm keeps going back, rather than stepping out; stay on the front leg and push off it to recover to the middle.

faults.name: Being upright on the front leg
faults.looks_like: Coming up to the ball standing tall and already on the front leg, with little body weight transfer through the shot.
faults.why_it_matters: You cannot extend further or move weight through the ball, so the contact point is short and the swing goes across the body.
causes: Not getting low with the legs
Being on the front leg before the swing starts
Reaching or stepping into the ball with only the front leg instead of getting there with the body
fixes: Get low with bent legs and the front heel down
Spread weight evenly on both legs, then transfer forward
Crouch and extend in a U shape
Bend the back leg more
Use a side step or crossover step to reach farther balls, then hit

faults.name: Hitting across the body
faults.looks_like: The swing and rotation travel across the body instead of linearly through the shot, with the non-hitting arm just hanging.
faults.why_it_matters: It gets rid of the ball across the body, so you lose control and topspin lift.
causes: Already extended on the front leg with no more room to go forward
Non-hitting arm hanging rather than moving back
Over-rotating
fixes: Move the left arm back as the racket arm goes forward
Hold a definite finish with the left arm behind
Transfer body weight forward through the shot
Keep rotating the legs on wide balls without swinging across

faults.name: Using the arm for power
faults.looks_like: The arm drives the ball, with a quick contact and no clear finish.
faults.why_it_matters: The hand and wrist cannot also create spin, so the shot is flatter and looks effortful.
causes: Not using body weight and legs
Short, rushed contact
fixes: Let body weight give the power
Extend, hold the ball on the strings, and keep the swing smooth
Slow the whole motion down
Let the wrist and hand add spin

faults.name: Rushing or stretching to meet the ball
faults.looks_like: Going too far forward or stretching for the ball instead of letting it come.
faults.why_it_matters: It disrupts balance and timing.
causes: Not trusting there is enough time
fixes: Let the ball come to you
Get closer to the ball with the legs
Stay nice and calm

faults.name: Lifting the racket arm to create spin / low finish position confusion
faults.looks_like: Finishing with the arm lifting the ball rather than the racket head swinging around the hand.
faults.why_it_matters: Spin should come from the racket head moving around the hand.
causes: Trying to lift the ball with the arm
fixes: Finish high with the racket head going around the hand after the low-to-high body move

faults.name: Stepping out instead of rotating on wide balls
faults.looks_like: Stepping out and shifting body weight off the front leg after hitting a wide ball.
faults.why_it_matters: You must change weight again to recover, so recovery is slower.
causes: Moving the legs out rather than rotating
fixes: Rotate out through the legs and push off the front leg to recover to the middle
outcome_effects: Being off balance on wide balls

faults.name: Keeping the back leg straight
faults.looks_like: Back leg is straight and the hip is locked.
faults.why_it_matters: The hip cannot rotate and the front knee and hip cannot move forward, so the weight transfer is hard.
causes: Not bending the back knee
fixes: Bend the back leg to get lower and move from back leg to front leg

good_form: Finish with the racket tip up and the racket circling around, with a closed racket face on the two-handed backhand.
Tilt the strings down at contact and swing up so the ball gets topspin and dips down into the court.
Close the racket face before contact so it stays square to the back of the ball as you brush and spin it.
Swing low to high, spinning up the back of the ball.
For a right-hander, keep the racket to the left of your hands through contact and the lift. This is the left side of the letter V.
A lefty keeps the racket to the right of the hands. The speaker also says to keep the racket on the hitting side of the hands.
Keeping the racket on that side keeps the wrist angle intact, with no play in the wrist. The strings then face the target longer.
Don't roll the racket over, so the direction the strings point doesn't change.
You can finish up high, as Fritz does, or let the racket drop, as Djokovic does. In both cases the racket stays on the correct side of the hands.
Use the same technique crosscourt as down the line. The speaker says it applies to one-handers and two-handers.

faults.name: Rolling the racket over / casting the wrist
faults.looks_like: On the follow-through the left wrist casts over and the racket moves to the right side of the hands (the right side of the V). The strings end up pointing down, and the wrists fly around.
faults.why_it_matters: The speaker says it makes you inconsistent. Keeping the racket on the left side is one of the top two or three ways to gain backhand consistency.
causes: Letting the left wrist cast over and the wrists fly after contact
Thinking of the finish only as touching the back after the hit
fixes: Keep the racket to the left of the hands (left side of the V) as you lift up after contact.
Keep the racket on the hitting side of the hands so the wrist angle stays intact.
Instead of thinking about touching your back, think about keeping the racket on the left of your hands as you go up.
Stop at the Fritz-style finish or let the racket drop like Djokovic, but keep the racket on the correct side.
outcome_effects: The strings point down and change direction instead of facing the target longer

good_form: Prepare early: turn the shoulders as the ball comes, with the shoulder ending under the chin.
Stay on your feet and keep moving into the shot.
Keep the grip loose, about a 3 out of 10 in tightness, with the hands feeling free.
Throw the racket head out in front as if throwing a heavy racket; the arms follow it.
Let the racket go back and down, let the hands pull, then throw the head once they are full.
The non-hitting hand passes over the hitting hand and takes control.
Keep the preparation short and the swing deep out in front.
Use an open stance, which keeps the backswing from going too far back.
Hit the ball high over the net with a loopy trajectory.

faults.name: Late preparation
faults.looks_like: The player turns and sets up late as the ball arrives, instead of turning the shoulders first.
faults.why_it_matters: The backhand itself is good, but late preparation is the thing holding it back.
fixes: Turn the shoulders first when the ball is fast.
Get the shoulder under the chin early.

faults.name: Tight grip
faults.looks_like: The player holds the racket handle tightly, at about a 5 out of 10.
faults.why_it_matters: The hands need to feel free to play the shot.
fixes: Drop the grip pressure to about 3 or 2 out of 10.
Imagine throwing the racket and letting the arms follow.
Let the hands go loose and pull, then throw the racket head.

faults.name: Backswing too long and finish too short
faults.looks_like: The player takes the racket very far back and then does not swing deep out in front.
faults.why_it_matters: The aim is a short preparation and a deep swing through the front.
causes: Using a closed stance lets the player go much further back.
fixes: Keep the open stance so you can't go as far back.
Keep the preparation short, then continue deep out in front.

faults.name: Flat ball over the net
faults.looks_like: The ball goes over the net on a flat, direct line instead of high.
faults.why_it_matters: The speaker wants the ball to go high over the net.
fixes: Find a way to hit a loopy ball that goes high over the net.
outcome_effects: The ball does not have the high, loopy shape the speaker wants.

good_form: Use an Eastern backhand grip, with the knuckle on the edge of the bevel; slide over from the forehand grip but not too far.
Start from a semi-western forehand grip and slide it over easily to the backhand grip.
Closed-stance sequence: turn, keep head on the ball, step, follow through, then recover.
Turn the shoulders and hips fully so the big body muscles power the shot, not just the arms; you may see part of your back.
The racket goes back naturally as you turn the shoulders; little extra movement is needed.
Stay in a low, athletic position with the legs engaged.
Keep feet moving with short steps while the ball approaches, then step into the ball.
Visualize the contact point out in front and try to see the ball hit the strings.
Keep head down and body level until after contact; the head comes up only after hitting.
Let the hands follow through with the arms, with the foot coming around; avoid excess wrist.
Always recover after the shot, even if it looks like a winner.
Open stance (advanced): turn and hit without stepping, to disguise the shot, when on the run, or on approach shots; still stay low.

faults.name: Sliding the grip too far
faults.looks_like: Moving the hand too far over from the Eastern backhand position, so the grip becomes more like a baseball grip.
faults.why_it_matters: The grip no longer sits properly on the bevel for a backhand.
fixes: Keep the knuckle on the edge of the bevel in the Eastern grip.
outcome_effects: Shot feels like a baseball swing

faults.name: Head and body popping up
faults.looks_like: Lifting the head and then the body up before or during contact instead of staying low and level.
faults.why_it_matters: You lose control and consistency, especially under pressure.
causes: Head comes up early, which brings the body up
fixes: Stay in the low athletic position through the turn and step
Keep the head down until contact, then let it come up
Visualize the contact point in front
outcome_effects: Inconsistent shots, especially when things get tight

faults.name: Standing planted waiting for the ball
faults.looks_like: Feet not moving as the ball approaches.
faults.why_it_matters: You cannot adjust to a bad bounce.
causes: Planted feet
fixes: Keep feet moving with short steps, then step into the ball
outcome_effects: Unable to move to a funny bounce

faults.name: No turn, just bunting the ball
faults.looks_like: Not turning the shoulders and just poking or bunting the ball, using only the arms.
faults.why_it_matters: You might get the ball in but will not improve long term.
causes: Beginners just wanting to get the ball back
fixes: Turn the shoulders, prep, and step into the shot

faults.name: Too much wrist or risk
faults.looks_like: Using lots of wrist and taking big risks on the swing.
faults.why_it_matters: The swing should be simple, with hands following the arms.
fixes: Let the hands follow through with the arms

faults.name: Not recovering
faults.looks_like: Stopping after the shot, assuming it was a winner.
faults.why_it_matters: The ball may come back and you will not be ready.
causes: Assuming the shot is a winner
fixes: Always recover after every shot
outcome_effects: Caught out if the ball returns

good_form: Turn the shoulders first, before anything else, using the non-dominant hand to pull the racket back while the hitting hand rests lightly on the grip.
Keep the racket head pointing up in the preparation so its drop can create topspin.
Keep the hitting arm bent in preparation; keeping the non-dominant hand close to the body makes the arm bend naturally.
Turn first, then move to the ball; footwork depends on which eye is dominant.
Right-eye dominant: last step on the right leg, planted in front of the left, foot at about 45 degrees to the net.
Left-eye dominant: land on the left leg so the dominant eye still faces the court; with no time, hit open stance, and with time, step the right foot in front.
Let the racket drop, then extend the arm forward in a slapping or Frisbee-throw motion (bend, extend), with the hand relaxed so the racket head falls and re-accelerates by itself.
The hand first travels one way and gradually turns to face the net, bringing the racket head with it.
Contact point for left-eye dominant is further forward, around or in front of the front foot; for right-eye dominant it is between the feet, closer to the front foot.
At contact, drive the ball by keeping it on the strings as long as possible for control; for spin, use a slightly tilted racket face that brushes the ball while still staying on the strings longer.
After the ball leaves the strings, release and let the racket finish loose, naturally up and far back.
The non-dominant arm moves backward as the hitting arm goes forward, opening the chest and keeping the shoulders aligned with the ball, including for down-the-line shots.
Finish the preparation by the time the ball bounces on your side, so you can accelerate and hit then, with the contact point in front and weight transferring forward.
On fast balls, shorten the preparation: keep the hand near the knee and just accelerate.
On high balls, step in and take the ball early on the rise rather than waiting and hitting over the shoulder; slice or flat shots can be mixed.

faults.name: Straight hitting arm in preparation
faults.looks_like: The hitting arm is held fully straight during the backswing, as Thiem and Robredo do.
faults.why_it_matters: The arm can't extend to accelerate, and it's very hard to move fast to different kinds of balls.
causes: The non-dominant hand goes far from the body, so the arm ends up straight
fixes: Keep the non-dominant hand close to the body so the hitting arm bends naturally

faults.name: Wrong footwork for eye dominance
faults.looks_like: A left-eye dominant player lands on the right leg with shoulders turned, so the dominant eye faces sideways instead of the court.
faults.why_it_matters: It becomes almost impossible to watch the court and ball with the left eye.
causes: Using the right-eye-dominant footwork pattern when left-eye dominant
fixes: Left-eye dominant players land on the left leg; use open stance if short on time
outcome_effects: Poor view of the ball and court

faults.name: No role for the non-dominant arm
faults.looks_like: The non-dominant arm stays in place instead of moving back and opening the chest during the shot.
faults.why_it_matters: The shoulders turn too early and too much, so the body has no control.
causes: Playing only with the hitting arm
fixes: Swing the non-dominant arm backward as the hitting arm goes forward, opening the chest and keeping the shoulders aligned with the ball

faults.name: Gripping too tight and no hand acceleration
faults.looks_like: The racket is held tightly and the player hits with the shoulder rather than accelerating the hand.
faults.why_it_matters: Hand acceleration is key and creates topspin and angles.
causes: Tension in the hand
fixes: Keep the hand relaxed and let the racket accelerate in a slapping motion
Practice drills with the preparation cut so you must create acceleration from a relaxed hand

faults.name: Starting preparation after the bounce
faults.looks_like: The player begins preparing only once the ball has bounced.
faults.why_it_matters: The timing is late and the body weight goes backward rather than forward.
causes: Late preparation
fixes: Have the preparation completely finished when the ball bounces, so the bounce is the cue to accelerate

faults.name: Taking high balls over the shoulder
faults.looks_like: Waiting for a high-bouncing ball and hitting it over the shoulder.
faults.why_it_matters: The one-hander tires, loses efficiency and is easier to attack, as Nadal showed against Federer.
causes: Waiting for the ball to drop instead of taking it early
fixes: Step in and take the ball early on the rise, mixing slice or flat shots
outcome_effects: Short replies that can be attacked

good_form: The backhand has four stages: unit turn, acceleration part one, acceleration part two (contact), and follow through.
In the unit turn, rotate the whole body as a unit with both hands on the racket, finishing in a set checkpoint.
Bend the knees anywhere from 20° to 90°, matching the level of the ball: bend more for low balls, less for high balls.
Rotate hips and trunk at least 90°, whether the stance is semi-open or closed.
At the end of the unit turn the dominant arm is fully straight, 10–20° away from the body, with a neutral wrist.
Dominant hand uses a Continental grip, index knuckle on bevel two.
Racket is slightly on edge or a little closed, tip about 45° up and away from the hand.
Non-dominant hand uses a mild Eastern or semi-western grip (bevel 3.5 to 4).
Non-dominant elbow is bent 90°, raised about 45°, and held about 10° inside the body.
Accelerate from the kinetic chain rather than the arms: shift weight forward, drive off the front leg, and rotate hips and trunk.
Pull the dominant arm away and down by abducting and extending it, using the lat and posterior deltoid.
Keep the wrists very relaxed. Consciously use the legs, core, hips and shoulders, and the wrist angles follow on their own.
The dominant wrist flexes in about 45° and ulnar deviates, so the racket drops beneath the hand.
Non-dominant arm straightens the elbow and pulls forward and away from the body (horizontal shoulder adduction), helping create the racket flip.
At the lowest point of the flip, the arms go from travelling down to travelling up and forward while the non-dominant arm internally rotates.
At contact the non-dominant wrist stays extended with the palm facing the net, to give power and spin from shoulder internal rotation.
At contact the trunk and hips are rotated about 45° in line with the net post. The amount varies with early or crosscourt hitting versus down the line.
For a topspin follow through, keep the strings in line with the net at contact and internally rotate the racket to finish.
For a flatter shot, as Djokovic does, let the racket open slightly and extend it forward and through instead of brushing up.

faults.name: Accelerating with the arms
faults.looks_like: Power comes from the arms instead of the legs, hips and trunk.
faults.why_it_matters: Top players generate natural, effortless power from the kinetic chain, not the arms.
causes: Focusing on the arms to accelerate rather than the body
fixes: Shift weight forward and drive off the front leg.
Rotate the hips and trunk at the same time.
Pull the right arm away and down using the lat and posterior deltoid.

faults.name: Tense wrists during acceleration
faults.looks_like: The small muscles of the wrist are actively tightened during the swing.
faults.why_it_matters: Relaxed wrists let the natural angles happen: wrist flexion and ulnar deviation, with the racket dropping beneath the hand.
causes: Focusing on the small muscles instead of the big muscles
fixes: Consciously contract the legs, core, hips and shoulders and keep the wrist as relaxed as possible.
outcome_effects: Optimal racket flip and angles are not reached
